title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Water Utilities | MPI
description: Mag particle testing of weld cracks on water tanks, steel pipe, penstocks and plant steelwork for US utilities. Technicians travel to your site. Get a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Water and Wastewater Utilities
html:
Magnetic particle inspection for water and wastewater utilities in the United States finds surface cracks in welds on steel tanks, steel pipe, penstocks, pump station piping and plant steelwork, most often right after abrasive blasting and just before the new coating goes on. Atlantis mobilizes SNT-TC-1A qualified technicians to your tank site or plant, examines the welds and repairs you identify, and returns a report with each indication on a sketch. To scope the work, request a magnetic particle inspection quote.

Why the blast-and-recoat window is the right time for MPI

Water utility steel spends most of its life under paint or lining, and a weld crack under intact coating is invisible. Rehabilitation changes that. When a tank interior or exterior is abrasively blasted to bare metal, every weld is exposed, and a magnetic particle examination on freshly blasted steel is clean, quick and sensitive. Doing the examination after blasting and before the primer is applied means any repair is made once, under the same containment, with the coating contractor already on site.

The method is simple in principle. A magnetic field is induced in the steel, a crack that reaches the surface disturbs the field, and fine ferromagnetic particles gather at the disturbance. It works only on ferromagnetic material and shows only surface and near-surface flaws, so thickness questions go to the UT page for water utilities, and stainless or other nonmagnetic equipment goes to the PT page.

Tank welds: shell seams, floor corners and attachments

Welded steel water tanks built to AWWA D100 carry long vertical and horizontal shell seams, a shell-to-floor connection, roof plate and rafter or column connections, and many welded attachments. AWWA D101 covers inspecting and repairing steel water tanks and describes what to look for. The weld areas that deserve a magnetic particle examination are the ones with high restraint or fatigue loading: the shell-to-bottom weld, nozzle and manway reinforcement welds, ladder and platform clips, and any repair weld.

In cold regions, ice formation in a tank can load the shell and attachments in ways the design did not anticipate, and cracking at attachments and weld toes is a recurring finding after such events. In earthquake country, the examination concentrates on anchor chair welds on tanks with anchor bolts and on shell-to-floor welds after a shaking event. We describe what we see and where; the utility's engineer interprets cause and consequence.

For elevated tanks, the tubular riser, column-to-bowl connections and bracing gusset welds are examined from the access the utility provides, and our tank inspection page describes how a full condition assessment fits together.

Steel pipe, penstocks and field welds

AWWA C200 covers steel water pipe, and AWWA Manual M11 is the engineer's design guide. Large-diameter steel mains and penstocks often use field-welded joints, and AWWA C206 addresses field welding of steel water pipe. Those field welds, along with branch connections, outlet reinforcement and repair welds, are the examination targets when pipe is exposed in a vault, crossing or excavation. Interior welds on large-diameter pipe are examined from inside under your confined space program after lining has been removed at the weld area.

Because the pipe is ferromagnetic carbon steel, a yoke gives good sensitivity on a cleaned weld. The technician examines the weld and the heat-affected zones on either side, in two directions across the weld, and marks each indication on the pipe and the sketch. Pipe diameter, curvature and access determine yoke handling, so the quote asks for the pipe size and the clear working space in the vault or trench.

Pump stations, digesters and clarifier steelwork

Pump station discharge headers, valve connection welds, pipe supports and lifting lugs are routine MT targets. In wastewater plants, clarifier center columns, drive supports, sludge collector structural steel and digester tank and cover welds are examined where corrosion, vibration or load cycling put welds under strain. Wastewater digesters can contain flammable and toxic gas, and any entry or hot work there follows the plant's permit system and gas monitoring.

Welded lifting attachments on pump stations and plant equipment are another frequent request. If the utility lifts heavy pumps, motors or gates, the rigger or engineer may require examination of welded lugs before use, and the MT report records each lug by identification and the result. The decision to use or replace a lug belongs to the rigger or engineer.

Technique details for utility steel

  • Surface condition. Blasted bare steel is ideal. Coating, rust scale and weld spatter reduce sensitivity, so the scope states who prepares each weld and to what level.
  • Yoke and field direction. An AC electromagnetic yoke is used on site, with the lifting-force check recorded at the start of work, and each area is examined in two perpendicular directions as ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E709 describe.
  • Contrast. On blasted steel, dry powder or wet visible particles are common outdoors. Where the work is in a dark tank, fluorescent particles under ultraviolet light are an option, and the ambient light and lamp intensity are recorded.
  • Coatings. Thin intact coatings can be examined through when the technique is demonstrated on known indications, but heavy or damaged coating is removed.
  • Cleanliness for potable service. Particles and carrier liquid are removed after examination so the coating system and disinfection steps can proceed, and the utility's procedure governs final cleanliness.
  • Temperature. Sun-heated steel in summer can exceed limits for liquid carriers, so dry methods or early-shade scheduling may be proposed.

Codes, regulators and acceptance

AWWA D100 and D101 for tanks, AWWA C200 and C206 and Manual M11 for steel pipe, and ASME Section V Article 7 for the examination method are the documents most often named in utility scopes. The Safe Drinking Water Act frames the regulatory context for public systems, and state drinking water programs enforce it. Acceptance criteria come from the construction standard the utility specifies, and the engineer of record decides whether to repair, recoat or replace. Atlantis reports what the examination found against the criteria in the scope, and we do not calculate remaining life, set intervals or decide fitness for service.

MT, UT or PT for water utility steel

Choosing a method for utility steel
QuestionMethodReason
Cracks at weld toes or repairs on carbon steelMTFerromagnetic and open to the surface
How much wall is left on a shell or pipeUTMT shows no thickness
Stainless chemical feed piping weldPTNot magnetic
Weld under heavy coatingRemove coating, then MTHeavy coating blocks the field
Cracks below the surfaceNot MTNeeds a volumetric method

What the report contains

The report identifies the tank, pipe segment or equipment and each weld examined, with the procedure and revision, the yoke and its lifting-force check, the particle type and carrier, surface condition, and the technician and SNT-TC-1A level. Indications appear on a sketch with location, orientation and length, and the report records acceptance or rejection against the criteria named in the scope. An ASNT Level III reviews the report before issue, and any weld not examined, with the reason, is listed.

What to send for a quote

  • Asset list with drawings, weld maps or plate layouts, and the design standard
  • Material and thickness, and whether any component is stainless, ductile iron or other nonmagnetic material
  • Weld locations of concern, past repairs and any known cracking history
  • Coating condition, lead content if known, and who blasts or cleans the welds
  • Whether the asset will be drained and out of service
  • Access arrangements and entry permit process
  • Site address and any security or background requirements

Scheduling around utility operations

Tank rehabilitation is planned around seasonal demand, and MPI sits between blasting and priming. Entry into tanks, vaults and wet wells follows 29 CFR 1910.146, or the construction confined space rules where the work is a construction project, together with your own permit procedure. Atlantis technicians travel to your site with yokes, particles, lamps and verification tools. The utility or its contractor provides power, lighting, access and ventilation, and the examination is scheduled once the date the blasted steel will be available is confirmed.

Where we work in the US for water and wastewater utilities

  • Phoenix, Arizona: canal-fed treatment plants, elevated tanks and desert reservoirs.
  • Tucson, Arizona: ground storage and booster stations across a wide service area.
  • Los Angeles, California: large-diameter steel conduits and seismic-zone tanks.
  • San Diego, California: coastal tanks and imported-water pipelines.
  • Denver, Colorado: cold-climate tanks that can see ice loading.
  • Salt Lake City, Utah: tanks and conduits in earthquake country.
  • El Paso, Texas: border-region storage and pump stations.
  • Albuquerque, New Mexico: reservoirs and booster stations at elevation.
  • Atlanta, Georgia: older steel standpipes and elevated tanks.
  • Dallas, Texas: large treated-water systems and plant steelwork.
  • Austin, Texas: hilltop elevated tanks and pump stations.

Training utility staff in MT

Utilities with welding and maintenance crews sometimes want their own surface examiners. MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training follow SNT-TC-1A, the magnetic particle simulator gives practice before live work, and your utility certifies its personnel under its own written practice. Procedure support is available through procedure development. For reading, see the magnetic particle testing guide and the page on magnetic particle testing.

What we do not do here

Atlantis does not perform radiography in the US, does not provide diver or underwater examination, and does not run in-line tools through pipelines. For weld-specific scopes beyond MT, see weld inspection.

faq.q: When is the best time to do MPI on a water tank?
faq.a: Right after abrasive blasting and before primer, because the welds are bare, clean and fully exposed. A crack found then is repaired under the same containment and the coating contractor already on site.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle testing be used on ductile iron or stainless pipe?
faq.a: Not reliably. Ductile iron is weakly or only partly magnetic in practice, and austenitic stainless is not magnetic. Surface cracks in those materials are examined with liquid penetrant where the surface allows.

faq.q: Do you examine through the tank coating?
faq.a: Thin intact coating can sometimes be examined through when the technique is proven on known indications under the same coating. Heavier or damaged coating is removed at the weld, and the procedure states the maximum thickness allowed.

faq.q: How do you handle potable water contact after MPI?
faq.a: Particles and carrier liquid are removed after examination so they do not remain on surfaces that will be coated and disinfected. The utility's own cleaning and disinfection procedure governs final cleanliness before the tank returns to service.

faq.q: Who decides whether an indication means repair?
faq.a: The utility's engineer of record applies the construction standard and decides. Atlantis records each indication with location, orientation and length against the criteria in the scope, and does not decide repair scope or fitness for service.

faq.q: Can you examine field welds on large-diameter steel pipe?
faq.a: Yes, on exposed pipe in vaults, crossings or excavations, and on interior welds when the lining is removed at the weld and entry follows your confined space permit. We need the pipe diameter and working space to plan yoke access.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote MPI on a tank or pipeline project?
faq.a: Send the asset list, drawings, weld locations of concern, material, coating status including lead content, drain and entry plans, access method and site address with any security steps. That lets us set coverage and technician days.

faq.q: Is MT the right method for finding corrosion loss?
faq.a: No. Magnetic particle shows surface cracks, not wall loss. For thickness and corrosion mapping, the ultrasonic thickness work on our UT page is the right method, and the two surveys can share one mobilization.

faq.q: Do you bring your own equipment?
faq.a: Yes. Technicians travel to your site with yokes, particle supplies, lamps and verification tools. The utility or its contractor provides power, lighting control, ventilation and access, and manages entry permits.
